idiom_name: stage plan: cheap handle first, remaining parts on demand, shared expensive part behind a guard
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the stages before writing code - the cheap part that is always acquired (descriptor, index, header, metadata, stub), the boundary a consumer may not cross for free, and the expensive parts that are fetched only when demanded. Acquire stage 1 eagerly and make it self-describing: it must answer existence, size, type, version and permission questions without touching the expensive part. Gate later stages on the real constraints (remaining memory, available connections, quota, deadline, back-pressure) and fetch in bounded parts, so that the second stage can never silently turn into a full acquisition. When several holders need the same expensive part, acquire it once behind a guard and share it instead of repeating the stage. Define the partial state explicitly: which operations are legal after stage 1, what happens when a later stage fails (roll back, continue with the part that is available, or abandon), and how every acquired stage is released - in reverse order, idempotently. Keep the plan visible in logs and metrics (parts fetched, bytes moved, rows read), because the cost model of a staged resource is a sum over stages rather than a constant.
code_sketch:
plan = [cheap(eager), expensive(on_demand, bounded), shared(once)]
handle = acquire(plan.cheap)              # always taken, always cheap
if not consumer.needs_more(handle): return handle
if plan.shared_needed: share(plan.shared) # one acquisition for all holders
for part in fetch(plan.rest, gated, bounded): consume(part)
release(reversed(acquired))               # reverse order, idempotent
pitfalls: Two stages in name only: if the first stage is not genuinely cheap and self-describing, the pattern degenerates into two eager acquisitions.
No release rule: every stage must be releasable, otherwise a partially acquired resource is a leak with extra steps.
Unguarded shared stage: concurrent holders each acquire the expensive part unless a once-guard, pool or cache sits in front of it.

Wrong move: treat every range or batch request as free random access -> fixed per-request overhead and backend round trips dominate -> instead choose bounded chunks and prefetch only when measured consumption justifies it.

Wrong move: retain a cursor, signed URL or one-shot body handle across an unbounded delay -> the provider expires or reaps the deferred stage -> instead bound the freshness window and re-resolve or re-authenticate before advancing.

Wrong move: expose a framework's partially initialized object as complete state -> later reads observe missing fields or trigger unbounded queries -> instead expose staged operations explicitly and use a bounded fetch plan for the needed fields.
